Reflections on the last year of AI security incidents: new attack techniques, the same failures they keep exploiting, and why AI security engineering is now a core discipline.

## Overview

Recently I’ve seen a lot of talk about exciting opportunities for AI security engineers: prompt injection, Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool poisoning, RAG poisoning, guardrails, automated red teaming, model extraction and interpretability. Many of these discussions and posts have focused on what people like to work on as opposed to the business requirements .

I want to do a reality check on what businesses need compared with what people want to work on. The job is to prevent loss and strengthen security (simplified), so that is where I start. This post covers the areas I find most important for AI security engineering today, each tied to what it protects a business from. It draws on a year of public incidents, attacker reports and hiring data.

So, in this post I will dive into my reflections on the wider AI security engineering landscape, holistically. My main takeaway is that the ways to attack are new, and the failures they exploit are the same ones we have had on our lists for years. I mean things like credentials left where an agent can read them, permissions that are too wide, no separation between staging and production, and backups inside the blast radius.

I started coding around the age of 12, which is about 30 years ago now, and started exploring security around 16, some 26 years ago. That was an interest long before it was a career. I was a kid exploring the internet in the era of online forums you had to reach from your dial-up modem, and around the turn of the millennium I was a moderator of one of the largest security forums online at the time. Security was always fun, and it was a gray hat phase for me. I loved securing things, but to secure something we first had to figure out how it could be exploited, so I had one foot in each camp. When capture the flag challenges became a thing I absolutely loved them: a safe environment where you get to exploit real systems. All of it taught me how attackers think, and that has helped me throughout my professional career, because every time we need to think about defense, I start by asking how I would get in.

From around 2018 I stepped further into leadership and was no longer only a hands-on engineer, and the compliance side of security came with that. I have worked a lot with SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 and GDPR in the years since, and the EU AI Act is now on the same list. I wrote about the mindset back then in Embracing the Security Development Lifecycle on Azure and Establish your organizational compliance readiness , and most of it still holds. Today my work is a solid blend of engineering leadership and hands-on building, and AI is what gave me the hands-on half back.

The attacker’s view matters as much now as it did then. Attackers are using AI agents, so I think we have to embrace agentic offensive security ourselves and learn how an AI-driven attacker works before we decide how to defend against one. That threat is growing fast, and I come back to it in Think like the attacker’s agent further down.

I write about working with coding agents in my agentic AI engineering series . The one opinion from it that matters most for this post is that a rule in a markdown file is a request and only something that can deny is a control, which I argue in why instructions aren’t enough for coding agents .

So, on with this post. Here’s what really got me thinking hard about the security landscape today, and how I think about the job.

To set the scene, I’m lining up some of the known incidents and research findings I’ve come across. This helps me paint the picture of why the rest of this article is important for anyone working with AI, especially if you’ve got access to sensitive systems or data, and if you’re interested in an AI security engineering type of job.

- An AI lab’s evaluation agents escaped their sandbox and broke into another company’s production infrastructure. OpenAI and Hugging Face, July 2026. During an internal cyber capability evaluation, OpenAI’s models got out through a previously unknown vulnerability in a package registry proxy , the sandbox’s only allowed network path, and went after the benchmark’s answers at Hugging Face. Hugging Face’s technical timeline counts about 17,600 attacker actions between 9 and 13 July, up to a production secret holding 136 keys and cluster-admin on 2 internal clusters, and says the only customer content accessed was 5 datasets. The zero-days were new, and what let the agent keep going was familiar, by Hugging Face’s own account: a template injection in dataset processing, no admission policy against privileged pods, a single credential shared across clusters, and an alert that never paged the on-call team.

- A production database and its backups, deleted in 9 seconds. PocketOS, April 2026. A coding agent on a staging task found a Railway CLI token in an unrelated file and deleted the production database and its volume-level backups with one API call. The backups lived inside the volume that was deleted, and the data only came back when Railway stepped in and restored it. The model misbehaved, and the damage came from a token that was left where the agent could read it and worked across every environment, and from the backup design.

- A production database erased during a code freeze. Replit, July 2025. An agent erased a production database while an explicit code freeze was in place. Nothing separated the environment the agent worked in from the one that held customer data, and that separation is what Replit’s CEO promised to add afterwards .

- Internal company data that a single email could exfiltrate. Microsoft 365 Copilot, June 2025, known as EchoLeak and tracked as CVE-2025-32711. One crafted email could make Copilot send internal data out, per Aim Labs’ write-up and Microsoft’s advisory . Microsoft fixed it on its side and lists it as not exploited. The injection technique was novel, and the exposure came from an agent that held private data, read an attacker’s email and had a way to send data out. That combination is what Simon Willison calls the lethal trifecta , and taking away any one of the three stops the attack.

- A deployed agent that could pivot into the customer’s cloud project. Google Vertex AI, March 2026. Unit 42’s Double Agents research showed that the service agent behind a deployed AI agent had default permissions wide enough to reach into the customer’s project and beyond. Google’s fix was documentation and a recommendation to bring your own service account. OWASP’s exploit round-up for the first quarter of 2026 puts it down to the excessive default permissions the agent inherited.

- Tens of thousands of agents exposed to the internet, and a marketplace carrying hundreds of malicious skills. OpenClaw, February 2026. Researchers found admin interfaces on the public internet, a one-click remote code execution bug , and an unreviewed marketplace where 341 of 2,857 skills were malicious, all running with the user’s full permissions. Every one of those was a known problem before anyone put a model in the loop. Default configurations were the first item in the NSA and CISA top 10 misconfigurations I wrote about in 2023, and they still are.

- SSH keys, cloud credentials and API tokens harvested from developer machines. Shai-Hulud, since September 2025. A self-propagating npm supply chain worm, documented by ReversingLabs and answered by GitHub’s changes to npm publishing . A Shai-Hulud-style worm in February 2026 went a step further and planted a rogue MCP server whose tool descriptions tell the coding agent to read the SSH keys and cloud credentials itself. The fix has nothing AI-specific in it: lifecycle scripts off, tokens short-lived, credentials rotated, and the agent’s configuration reviewed like code.

- Human approval gates bypassed, more consistently than any other failure. Microsoft AI Red Team, June 2026. After a year of red teaming deployed agents, they reported that human-in-the-loop bypass was the failure mode they saw exploited most consistently . A gate the model can argue its way past, or that a tired human clicks through, does not hold. It is the reason I keep the hard lines on irreversible actions with me rather than with the agent.

The pattern I take from this is that the model is the new untrusted component in an old architecture . Everything we already know about untrusted components applies: least privilege, separate identities, separate environments, deny by default, confirmation before irreversible actions, backups outside the blast radius, logs that cannot be edited. What is new for me is having to know where the model sits in the data flow and which of those controls it can talk its way around, so that I build the ones it cannot.

I mentioned earlier that I start every defense by asking how I would get in. Over the last year, the people getting in started using AI agents to do it, and this is what that looked like in real intrusions.

Open-source offensive AI frameworks have multiplied over the last 2 years. These are some of the most popular, by GitHub stars as I write this:

- Strix , about 74,000 stars. Autonomous agents that test a running application and validate each finding with a proof of concept.

- Shannon , about 52,000 stars. A white-box pentester for web applications and APIs that reads the source code first and then exploits the running application.

- PentAGI , about 34,000 stars. A multi-agent system that runs penetration tests autonomously.

- PentestGPT , about 16,000 stars. The framework from the USENIX Security 2024 paper, which now runs autonomous pipelines on Claude Code or Codex.

- HexStrike , about 13,500 stars. An MCP server that exposes more than 150 security tools to any model.

- CAI , about 10,000 stars. A research framework from Alias Robotics, archived in August 2026.

- Cairn , about 5,000 stars. Worker agents that share findings on a common board, first tested on autonomous penetration testing.

- hackingBuddyGPT , about 1,300 stars. A research framework from TU Wien for privilege escalation, web and Active Directory testing.

- ARTEX, which has no link. Its developer took the repository down in October 2026 because attackers were using it in real intrusions, which makes it the best documented case of one of these tools being turned on businesses. More on it below.

All of them are built around someone else’s model, and most share one shape: a planner that turns a goal into steps, workers that run the ordinary tools, nmap, sqlmap, a browser, a cloud CLI, and a loop that keeps going until the goal is met or the budget runs out. The model is usually rented and the tooling underneath is decades old.

Three data points show where this went:

- XBOW, June 2025. It reached the top of HackerOne’s US leaderboard with nearly 1,060 reports, each reviewed by a human before submission.

- HexStrike, August 2025. It had been public for a few weeks when Citrix published 3 NetScaler CVEs, and Check Point watched criminal forums discussing it against those flaws within 12 hours, claiming exploitation time down from days to under 10 minutes. That claim is theirs and nobody has verified it, though Check Point did see lists of seemingly vulnerable hosts offered for sale.
